issues.legal_issue: Section 27 of the Evidence Act admits only information from an accused in police custody that distinctly and proximately leads to discovery of a previously unknown fact, including the physical object, its location, and the accused’s knowledge of its existence.
Police custody for the purposes of Section 27 of the Evidence Act includes police restraint, restriction, or surveillance and does not require formal arrest.

A discovery of a concealed dead body at a place identified by an accused may support an inference that the accused concealed it when the accused provides no credible explanation for the knowledge, once the prosecution has established its case through circumstantial evidence.

Section 106 of the Evidence Act permits an adverse inference from an accused’s failure to explain facts within their special knowledge only after the prosecution has established the relevant circumstances, and does not shift the prosecution’s burden of proof.
A conviction based on circumstantial evidence is sustainable where the proved circumstances form a complete chain that excludes reasonable hypotheses consistent with innocence.
An acquittal in a separate prosecution based on a different body of evidence does not negate the evidence supporting conviction in the present prosecution.
Information already disclosed by one accused cannot be used as a discovery under Section 27 of the Evidence Act against a co-accused, absent a joint disclosure.
